meta.subject: INTEGRATED_3
meta.author: bank-team-integrated-3
meta.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: List the sample space for a simple experiment
questions.stem: A coin is flipped twice; what is the sample space of ordered outcomes?

options.text: {HH, HT, TH, TT} listing all four ordered pairs
{HH, HT, TT} merging HT and TH as one outcome
{0,1,2} counting heads only
options.misconception: counts heads instead of listing outcomes

options.text: {H,T} ignoring the second flip

questions.explanation: Ordered flips give four distinct outcomes: HH, HT, TH, TT. Merging HT and TH or counting heads changes the sample space. Listing all ordered pairs avoids double counting.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize when outcomes are not equally likely
questions.stem: A loaded die has faces 1-6 with P(6)=1/2 and others equal; are all six outcomes equally likely?

options.text: Yes, a die always has six equally likely faces
options.misconception: assumes fair die regardless of loading

options.text: No, P(6) differs from the others
Yes, because the outcomes are still six distinct numbers
Cannot tell without rolling it many times

questions.explanation: Equal likelihood requires equal probabilities; here P(6)=1/2 while each other face gets 1/10, so they are not equal. Distinct outcomes alone do not guarantee fairness. The given probabilities settle it.

questions.learningObjective: Compute probability in a non-uniform space
questions.stem: In a bag with 2 red and 3 blue, P(red) is 2/5; explain why not 1/2.

answer.exemplar: There are 5 equally likely draws, 2 of which are red, so P(red)=2/5; treating colors as equally likely ignores counts.

questions.explanation: Probability is favorable over total equally likely outcomes: 2 red out of 5 total gives 2/5. Treating the two colors as equally likely ignores the differing counts. Counting items, not categories, fixes it.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish permutations from combinations
questions.stem: How many ways can 3 people be chosen from 5 for a committee (order irrelevant)?
questions.explanation: This is C(5,3)=5!/(3!2!)=10. Using permutations 5*4*3=60 would overcount by ordering. The key is whether order matters; here it does not.

questions.learningObjective: Test independence of two events
questions.stem: P(A)=0.4, P(B)=0.5, P(A and B)=0.2; is A independent of B? Encode 1 yes, 0 no.
questions.explanation: Independence requires P(A and B)=P(A)P(B)=0.4*0.5=0.2, which matches, so the answer is 1. The product rule is the test. A tempting error is to compare P(A) and P(B) directly.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret the sign and magnitude of r
questions.stem: A study reports r=-0.85 between hours studied and errors; what does it mean?

options.text: Strong positive association after squaring r
Weak negative association because r is below -1
options.misconception: thinks r must be below -1 to be strong

options.text: Strong negative linear association: more study links to fewer errors
No association because r is not exactly -1
options.misconception: requires perfect correlation for any association

questions.explanation: r=-0.85 is close to -1, indicating a strong negative linear association. Squaring gives r^2 but does not change the direction. Perfect correlation is not required for a strong association. The tempting errors are sign confusion or demanding r=-1.
questions.hint: Sign gives direction, magnitude gives strength.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a confounding variable
questions.stem: Ice cream sales and drowning deaths rise together; what explains the correlation?

options.text: Ice cream consumption causes drowning
The correlation is exactly zero after controlling
Drowning causes people to buy ice cream
Hot weather increases both ice cream sales and swimming

questions.explanation: A common cause, hot weather, drives both variables, creating spurious correlation. Neither variable causes the other. Controlling for temperature would remove the association. The tempting mistake is to infer causation from correlation.

questions.learningObjective: Encode a binary category numerically
questions.stem: For gender with values male/female, a coder assigns 1 and 2; what is the issue?

options.text: Categorical variables cannot be encoded at all
The codes should be 0 and 1 only
options.misconception: prefers a specific coding without reason

options.text: The codes imply an order and distance that do not exist
The codes are fine because any numbers work
options.misconception: ignores that arbitrary codes mislead models

questions.explanation: Assigning 1 and 2 suggests male < female with a meaningful gap, which is false for nominal categories. Any distinct codes work for labels, but ordered numbers mislead models. The tempting error is to say any numbers are fine.
questions.hint: Nominal codes should not imply order.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize an unsupported population claim
questions.stem: A sample of 50 volunteers from one school supports a claim about all teenagers; why not?

answer.exemplar: Volunteers from one school are not representative of all teenagers, so generalizing beyond the sampling frame is unsupported.

questions.explanation: The sampling frame is one school and volunteers self-select, so the sample may differ from all teenagers in age, region, and motivation. Generalizing beyond the frame is unsupported. A larger sample from the same frame would not fix representativeness.

questions.learningObjective: Identify an untestable assumption in a model
questions.stem: A model assumes errors are normally distributed; can this be verified from the data? Encode 1 yes, 0 no.
questions.explanation: Normality of errors is an assumption about unobserved population errors; data can only suggest, not prove, it. The answer is 0. The tempting error is to think a large sample proves normality. Diagnostics check plausibility, not truth.
questions.hint: Assumptions are not provable from data.

questions.learningObjective: Compute the size of a sample space
questions.stem: A password is 4 digits, each 0-9; how many possible passwords?
questions.explanation: Each of 4 positions has 10 choices, so 10^4 = 10000 possible passwords. The tempting error is 4*10=40. Multiplying independent choices gives the total.

questions.learningObjective: Compute probability with equally likely outcomes
questions.stem: A fair die is rolled; what is P(even)?

options.text: 1/6 because only 6 is even
1/3 because there are three even numbers
options.misconception: divides by number of favorable categories not total

options.text: 2/3 because even faces are larger
1/2 because three of six faces are even

questions.explanation: Three even faces out of six equally likely faces gives 3/6=1/2. Dividing by 3 or counting one face are common errors. Counting favorable over total fixes it.

questions.learningObjective: Compute probability from a frequency table
questions.stem: A table shows 40 red, 60 blue out of 100; what is P(blue)?

options.text: 0.4 because 40/100
0.6 because 60/100
0.5 because colors are two categories
60 because that is the count

questions.explanation: P(blue)=60/100=0.6. Using the red count or treating two colors as equally likely are common errors. Probability is count over total, not category over categories.

questions.learningObjective: Compute permutations of distinct items
questions.stem: How many ways can 4 distinct books be arranged on a shelf? Suki says 4+3+2+1=10; is she right?

options.text: No, it should be 4^4=256
Yes, arranging adds positions
No, arrangements multiply: 4*3*2*1=24
No, combinations give C(4,4)=1

questions.explanation: Arranging 4 distinct books is 4! = 24, found by multiplying 4*3*2*1. Adding positions or using combinations are common errors. Order matters here, so permutations apply.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why disjoint events are not independent
questions.stem: Why can two disjoint events with positive probability not be independent?

answer.exemplar: Disjoint means P(A and B)=0, but independence needs P(A)P(B)>0, so the product rule fails.

questions.explanation: If both have positive probability, their product is positive, but disjointness makes the intersection probability zero. Thus the product rule fails and they are dependent. Knowing one occurs rules out the other.

questions.learningObjective: Compute r squared from r
questions.stem: If r=0.6 between X and Y, what is r^2?
questions.explanation: r^2 = 0.6^2 = 0.36, meaning 36% of variance in Y is linearly explained by X. A tempting error is to take 0.6*2=1.2. Squaring, not doubling, gives the coefficient of determination.

questions.learningObjective: Identify reverse causation
questions.stem: A drug lowers blood pressure; patients with lower pressure take more drug; is the drug effect confounded? Encode 1 yes, 0 no.
questions.explanation: Reverse causation occurs when the outcome influences the treatment: lower pressure leads to more drug use, confounding the effect. The answer is 1. The tempting error is to assume the drug alone caused the change.

questions.learningObjective: Use one-hot encoding for a nominal variable
questions.stem: For color with values red/green/blue, which encoding is appropriate?

options.text: Count: number of colors present
Label: 1,2,3 implying an order
options.misconception: imposes false order on nominal colors

options.text: Binary: 0/1 for red vs not red only
One-hot: three binary columns, one per color

questions.explanation: One-hot encoding creates a binary column per category, avoiding false order. Label encoding imposes order, binary loses categories, and count is meaningless. The tempting error is to use 1,2,3 for simplicity.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize a claim beyond the data
questions.stem: A study of 200 adults aged 30-40 cannot support a claim about children; why?

options.text: 200 is too small for any conclusion
The sample excludes children, so generalization is invalid
Adults and children have the same traits
The study must be experimental, not observational

questions.explanation: The sampling frame is adults 30-40, so children are outside it and generalization is invalid. Sample size is not the issue; representativeness is. The tempting error is to blame n=200.

questions.learningObjective: Identify an uncheckable independence assumption
questions.stem: A model assumes observations are independent; can we verify this from the sample alone?

options.text: Yes, if the sample is random
options.misconception: confuses random sampling with independence of observations

options.text: Yes, compute the correlation among residuals
No, independence is an assumption about the data-generating process
No, but we can prove dependence instead
options.misconception: thinks dependence is provable when independence is not

questions.explanation: Independence concerns how data were generated, not just the sample values; a sample cannot prove it. Random sampling helps but does not guarantee independence of underlying observations. The tempting errors are residual checks or equating random sampling with independence.
questions.hint: Independence is about generation, not data.

questions.learningObjective: Compute probability of union of two events
questions.stem: P(A)=0.3, P(B)=0.4, P(A and B)=0.1; find P(A or B) and explain.

answer.exemplar: P(A or B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A and B)=0.3+0.4-0.1=0.6, subtracting the overlap once.

questions.explanation: The inclusion-exclusion formula gives 0.3+0.4-0.1=0.6. Adding without subtracting double counts the overlap. The tempting error is 0.7, which double counts the intersection.

questions.learningObjective: Compute probability of a complement
questions.stem: P(rain)=0.3; what is P(no rain)?
questions.explanation: Complement probability is 1 - 0.3 = 0.7. The tempting error is to report 0.3 again. Complements sum to 1, giving a quick check.

questions.learningObjective: Compute conditional probability in a non-uniform space
questions.stem: A box has 3 red, 7 blue; given the draw is not red, what is P(blue)?
questions.explanation: If not red then the draw is blue, since only red and blue exist, so P(blue | not red)=1. The tempting error is to compute 7/10=0.7, ignoring the condition. Conditioning on not red eliminates reds.

questions.learningObjective: Compute combinations with repetition
questions.stem: How many ways to choose 2 fruits from 3 types with repetition allowed?

options.text: 6 using 3*2
3 using 3 types only
9 using 3^2

questions.explanation: Combinations with repetition: C(n+k-1,k)=C(4,2)=6. Ordered counts overcount; choosing types only undercounts. The stars-and-bars formula gives 6. The tempting errors are 3^2 or 3*2.

questions.learningObjective: Compute probability of intersection under independence
questions.stem: If A and B are independent with P(A)=0.2, P(B)=0.5, what is P(A and B)?

options.text: 0.1 because 0.2*0.5
0.7 because 0.2+0.5
0.3 because 0.5-0.2
0.25 because (0.2+0.5)/2? no, 0.1 is correct; 0.25 is wrong

questions.explanation: Under independence, P(A and B)=P(A)P(B)=0.2*0.5=0.1. Adding or averaging probabilities are common errors. The product rule is the defining property of independence.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize that correlation is symmetric
questions.stem: A report says r(X,Y)=0.7 but r(Y,X)=-0.7; is this possible?

options.text: Yes, order of variables flips the sign
No, correlation is symmetric so r(Y,X)=0.7
Yes, if Y is the response variable
Cannot tell without the data

questions.explanation: Pearson r is symmetric: r(X,Y)=r(Y,X). The sign cannot flip with order. The tempting error is to treat the explanatory/response distinction as affecting correlation.
questions.hint: r is symmetric in X and Y.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish correlation from causation in a headline
questions.stem: A headline says 'Coffee drinkers live longer' from an observational study; what is the flaw?

answer.exemplar: Observational data cannot establish causation; confounders like income or health habits may explain the link.

questions.explanation: Observational studies show association, not causation. Confounding variables such as income or lifestyle could drive both coffee drinking and longevity. A randomized trial would be needed for a causal claim. The tempting error is to accept the headline.

questions.learningObjective: Avoid dummy variable trap
questions.stem: For 3 categories with one-hot encoding, how many columns avoid the dummy trap?
questions.explanation: With k categories, use k-1 dummy columns to avoid perfect multicollinearity; for 3 categories that is 2. Using all 3 creates the dummy variable trap. The tempting error is to use 3. Dropping one reference category fixes it.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize a claim about causation from observation
questions.stem: An observational study finds exercisers have lower BMI; can it support 'exercise reduces BMI'? Encode 1 yes, 0 no.
questions.explanation: Observational data cannot support a causal claim because confounders like diet or genetics may explain the association. The answer is 0. The tempting error is to accept the causal wording. A randomized experiment would be needed.

questions.learningObjective: Identify an uncheckable homoscedasticity assumption
questions.stem: A regression assumes constant variance of errors; is this verifiable from one sample?

options.text: Yes, if the sample is large enough
options.misconception: thinks large n proves the assumption

options.text: Yes, plot residuals vs fitted values
options.misconception: thinks a plot proves constant variance

options.text: No, it is an assumption about the error process
No, but heteroscedasticity is impossible

questions.explanation: Constant variance is an assumption about the unobserved error process; data can suggest but not prove it. Residual plots check plausibility, not truth. The tempting errors are to treat plots or large n as proof.

questions.learningObjective: List outcomes for a spinner
questions.stem: A spinner has sectors A,B,C; what is the sample space?

options.text: {A,B} omitting C
{A,B,C,AB,AC,BC} adding pairs
{1,2,3} numbering sectors
{A,B,C} the three sectors

questions.explanation: The sample space is the set of possible outcomes {A,B,C}. Adding pairs or renumbering changes it. Each spin yields exactly one sector.

questions.learningObjective: Check if a spinner is fair
questions.stem: A spinner has equal-area sectors A,B,C; are outcomes equally likely?

options.text: No, spinners are never fair
Yes, equal areas give equal probabilities
No, need to spin many times to know
Yes, because there are three sectors

questions.explanation: Equal areas imply equal probabilities for a well-constructed spinner, so outcomes are equally likely. Counting sectors alone would be wrong if areas differed. The given equal areas settle it.

questions.learningObjective: Compute probability from weighted outcomes
questions.stem: Outcomes have weights 2,3,5; what is P(first)? Explain.

answer.exemplar: Total weight is 10, so P(first)=2/10=0.2; probability is weight over total weight.

questions.explanation: Probability is weight divided by total weight: 2/(2+3+5)=0.2. Treating outcomes as equally likely would give 1/3, which is wrong. Weighted spaces need weighted counts.

questions.learningObjective: Compute permutations of a subset
questions.stem: How many ways to arrange 3 of 5 distinct books on a shelf?
questions.explanation: P(5,3)=5*4*3=60. Combinations C(5,3)=10 would undercount by ignoring order. The question asks for arrangements, so order matters and permutations apply.

questions.learningObjective: Compute P(A or B) for independent events
questions.stem: A,B independent with P(A)=0.2,P(B)=0.3; what is P(A or B)?
questions.explanation: P(A or B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A)P(B)=0.2+0.3-0.06=0.44. The tempting error is 0.5, which ignores the overlap. Independence gives the intersection as the product.

questions.learningObjective: Compare strengths of correlations
questions.stem: Which correlation is stronger: r=0.8 or r=-0.9?

options.text: They are equal because both are strong
r=0.8 because positive is stronger
r=-0.9 because magnitude 0.9 exceeds 0.8
Cannot compare different variables

questions.explanation: Strength is determined by absolute value; 0.9 > 0.8, so r=-0.9 is stronger regardless of sign. Positive is not inherently stronger. The tempting error is to prefer the positive correlation.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a lurking variable
questions.stem: Shoe size and reading ability correlate in children; what is the lurking variable?

options.text: There is no lurking variable; it is a real effect
Shoe size causes reading ability
Reading ability causes shoe size
Age, which affects both shoe size and reading

questions.explanation: Age drives both shoe size and reading ability, creating a spurious correlation. Neither variable causes the other. The tempting errors are causal claims or denying confounding.

questions.learningObjective: Encode an ordinal variable properly
questions.stem: For education level low/medium/high, is label encoding 1/2/3 appropriate?

options.text: No, any encoding must be one-hot
Yes, the order is meaningful so 1<2<3 fits
No, labels must be 0/1 only
No, order never matters in encoding

questions.explanation: Ordinal categories have a meaningful order, so 1<2<3 preserves it. One-hot is for nominal variables. The tempting errors are to require one-hot always or to deny order. The key distinction is nominal vs ordinal.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize a claim about a subgroup
questions.stem: A sample has 5% left-handed people; can it support a claim that 5% of all left-handed people are in the sample?

answer.exemplar: No, the sample proportion does not imply the reverse; sampling variability and frame limits prevent such a claim.

questions.explanation: The sample proportion estimates the population proportion, not the reverse. Confusing the two is a base-rate fallacy. The sampling frame and variability also limit the claim. The tempting error is to invert the proportion.

questions.learningObjective: Identify an uncheckable linearity assumption
questions.stem: A linear model assumes a straight-line relationship; can data prove linearity? Encode 1 yes, 0 no.
questions.explanation: Linearity is an assumption about the underlying relationship; data can suggest or contradict but not prove it. The answer is 0. Residual patterns can hint at nonlinearity but cannot confirm linearity. The tempting error is to treat a good fit as proof.

questions.learningObjective: Compute probability of at least one success
questions.stem: A fair coin is flipped 3 times; what is P(at least one head)?
questions.explanation: P(at least one head)=1-P(no heads)=1-(1/2)^3=1-1/8=7/8=0.875. The tempting error is 3/2, which exceeds 1. The complement is easier here.

questions.learningObjective: Compute probability with a fair spinner
questions.stem: A fair 4-sector spinner; what is P(landing on sector 2)?

options.text: 1 because sector 2 is certain
1/2 because sector 2 is half the spinner
1/4 because four equal sectors
1/3 because sectors 2 and 3 merge

questions.explanation: Four equal sectors give P=1/4 for any one sector. The tempting errors are to double the share or merge sectors. Equal areas ensure equal probabilities.

questions.learningObjective: Compute probability from a weighted spinner
questions.stem: A spinner has sectors with probabilities 0.2,0.3,0.5; what is P(second sector)?

options.text: 0.2 because sectors are ordered
1/3 because three sectors
0.5 because it is the middle sector
0.3 as stated

questions.explanation: The given probability for the second sector is 0.3. Treating three sectors as equally likely would give 1/3, which is wrong. The stated weights govern. The tempting error is to ignore the given probabilities.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish ordered from unordered selection
questions.stem: A committee of 3 from 5: does order of selection matter?

options.text: Yes, because members join in sequence
options.misconception: confuses selection process with final set

options.text: No, a committee is an unordered set
Yes, because each member has a rank
Cannot tell without more info

questions.explanation: A committee is an unordered set, so order does not matter and combinations apply. The selection process may have an order, but the result is a set. The tempting error is to confuse process with outcome.
questions.hint: Committee is a set, not a sequence.

questions.learningObjective: Compute probability under dependence
questions.stem: P(A)=0.4,P(B)=0.5,P(A and B)=0.1; are A,B independent? Explain.

answer.exemplar: P(A)P(B)=0.2, but P(A and B)=0.1, so they are not independent; the product rule fails.

questions.explanation: Independence requires P(A and B)=P(A)P(B)=0.2, but the actual intersection is 0.1, so the events are dependent. The tempting error is to compare 0.4 and 0.5 and declare independence. Checking the product resolves it.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret r near zero
questions.stem: If r=0.05 between X and Y, how strong is the linear association? Encode 0 none,1 weak,2 moderate,3 strong.
questions.explanation: r=0.05 is close to 0, indicating a very weak linear association, encoded as 1. The tempting error is to call it moderate because r is nonzero. Magnitude near 0 means weak.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a common response
questions.stem: Both ice cream sales and crime rise in summer; is this a common response? Encode 1 yes, 0 no.
questions.explanation: Both variables respond to a common cause (summer/heat), so this is a common response, encoded 1. The tempting error is to call it causation. Identifying the shared driver resolves it.

questions.learningObjective: Choose encoding for a high-cardinality variable
questions.stem: A variable has 500 distinct city names; which encoding is most practical?

options.text: Label encoding 1..500
options.misconception: imposes a false order on cities

options.text: One-hot with 500 columns
Target or frequency encoding to keep dimension small
Drop the variable entirely

questions.explanation: High-cardinality categoricals are better handled by target or frequency encoding to avoid 500 columns or false order. One-hot is too large, label encoding is misleading, and dropping loses information. The tempting error is one-hot by habit.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize a claim about a rare event
questions.stem: A sample of 100 has 0 cases of a rare disease; can it support P(disease)=0?

options.text: No, but only because the sample is biased
options.misconception: blames bias instead of sampling variability

options.text: Yes, 0/100 means the disease does not exist
options.misconception: equates sample zero with population zero

options.text: Yes, 100 is large enough for rare events
options.misconception: overestimates sample adequacy for rare events

options.text: No, absence of evidence is not evidence of absence

questions.explanation: Zero cases in 100 does not prove the disease is absent; a rare event may simply not appear. The issue is sampling variability, not necessarily bias. The tempting errors are to equate sample zero with population zero or to blame bias alone.
questions.hint: Rare events may not appear in small samples.

questions.learningObjective: Identify an uncheckable normality of predictors assumption
questions.stem: A model assumes predictors are normally distributed; is this required and checkable?

options.text: Required and checkable from histograms
Not required and not checkable as a model assumption
Required but not checkable
Not required but checkable
options.misconception: thinks we must verify predictor normality

questions.explanation: Linear regression does not require normally distributed predictors, and normality of errors is the relevant assumption. Predictor normality is neither required nor a model assumption. The tempting errors are to require or check predictor normality.

questions.learningObjective: Compute number of outcomes for two dice
questions.stem: Two fair dice are rolled; how many outcomes in the sample space? Explain.

answer.exemplar: Each die has 6 faces, so there are 6*6=36 ordered pairs in the sample space.

questions.explanation: Ordered pairs of two six-sided dice give 6*6=36 outcomes. Treating (1,2) and (2,1) as one would give 21, which is wrong for ordered dice. The sample space uses ordered pairs.

questions.learningObjective: Compute probability of a sum with two dice
questions.stem: Two fair dice are rolled; what is P(sum=7)?
questions.explanation: There are 6 ways to make 7 out of 36 outcomes, so P=6/36=1/6≈0.1667. The tempting error is 1/11, counting sums as equally likely. Sums are not equally likely; outcomes are.

questions.learningObjective: Compute probability from a biased coin
questions.stem: A biased coin has P(heads)=0.7; what is P(tails)?
questions.explanation: P(tails)=1-0.7=0.3. The tempting error is 0.7, repeating heads. Complements sum to 1 even for biased coins.

questions.learningObjective: Compute probability using combinations
questions.stem: From 5 people, 2 are chosen; what is P(a specific pair is chosen)?

options.text: 1/5 because one pair over five
2/5 because two people out of five
options.misconception: uses people over people instead of pairs

options.text: 1/C(5,2)=1/10 because one favorable pair out of 10
2/10 because two favorable orders

questions.explanation: There is 1 favorable pair out of C(5,2)=10 possible pairs, so P=1/10. Counting people or orders gives wrong denominators. Combinations count unordered pairs. The tempting error is 2/5.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish mutual exclusivity from independence
questions.stem: Which statement about mutually exclusive events with positive probability is true?

options.text: They are independent if one has probability 1
They are always independent
They are independent if probabilities sum to 1
They cannot be independent

questions.explanation: Mutually exclusive events with positive probability have intersection 0, but their product is positive, so they are dependent. Independence and mutual exclusivity are different concepts. The tempting error is to equate them.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize that r requires linear relationship
questions.stem: A scatterplot shows a perfect U-shape; r≈0; is there no relationship?

options.text: Yes, r≈0 means no relationship of any kind
No, r only measures linear association, not all relationships
Yes, because r^2≈0
Cannot tell without computing r

questions.explanation: r measures linear association only; a strong nonlinear U-shape can have r≈0. The tempting errors are to equate r≈0 with no relationship or to rely on r^2. Nonlinear patterns need other measures.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a confounder in an observational study
questions.stem: A study finds wine drinkers have better heart health; what confounder might explain this?

answer.exemplar: Socioeconomic status or overall lifestyle could confound, since wealthier people may drink wine and have better healthcare.

questions.explanation: Confounding variables such as socioeconomic status or lifestyle could drive both wine consumption and heart health. Observational data cannot separate them. A randomized trial would be needed for causation. The tempting error is to accept the causal claim.

questions.learningObjective: Encode a binary outcome for logistic regression
questions.stem: For a yes/no outcome, what numeric encoding is standard for logistic regression? Encode the lower value.
questions.explanation: Standard encoding is 0 for no and 1 for yes, so the lower value is 0. This keeps the log-odds interpretation clean. The tempting error is to use 1 and 2. Zero/one is conventional.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize an extrapolation beyond data
questions.stem: A linear fit on ages 20-40 predicts at age 80; is this reliable? Encode 1 yes, 0 no.
questions.explanation: Predicting far outside the observed range is extrapolation and is unreliable because the relationship may change. The answer is 0. The tempting error is to trust the fitted line everywhere. Staying within the data range is safer.

questions.learningObjective: Summarize why model assumptions are provisional
questions.stem: Why are statistical model assumptions always provisional?

options.text: They are unnecessary in modern statistics
They are proven by large samples
Data can support but never fully prove them
They are checked by p-values only

questions.explanation: Assumptions are about unobserved processes; data can support or contradict but never prove them. Large samples help but do not prove. The tempting errors are to treat large n or p-values as proof. Assumptions remain provisional.
